title: A Guru at five
hookLine: the youngest Guru takes up the task as a small child and is remembered for his calm

cards: A five-year-old can tie a shoe, mostly. They can tell you, at length, about a dinosaur. They cry when the sandwich is cut the wrong way.

Now put that child on a seat where grown men with long beards bow to him, and ask him to guide a whole community, while an older brother who thinks the job should be his watches, and an emperor wonders what kind of child this is.
That was Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, chosen in 1661 when his father, Guru Har Rai, died.

teach.h: GURU AT FIVE, GONE BY EIGHT.
teach.b: Guru Har Krishan became Guru at about five and lived only to about eight. So there are no great battles, and no hymns of his in the scripture. What Sikhs remember is his calm, and what came out of it.
His older brother Ram Rai, the one who changed the word, went to the emperor Aurangzeb and pressed his claim, and the child Guru was summoned to Delhi.

On the way, at a village called Panjokhara, tradition says a proud scholar challenged the boy: if you're really the Guru, explain the Gita, the great Hindu scripture, to me. The Guru didn't argue or show off.
He asked for someone from the village, and a humble water-carrier named Chhajju was brought, a man who had never studied.
The Guru touched him lightly with his stick, and Chhajju began to explain the Gita so deeply that the scholar was left silent, and humbled. Sikhs don't tell it as a trick.

They tell it as wisdom that doesn't depend on age or schooling: the child Guru pointed away from himself, to the person the scholar least expected. In Delhi he stayed at the house of a Rajput noble, Raja Jai Singh.
Tradition says the Raja's queen tested him by dressing as a maid among her servants, and the child walked straight to her. Tradition also says he declined to meet the emperor at all.
Small, calm, unimpressed by the powerful.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, in the daily Ardas, which says, in paraphrase, that at the sight of him all suffering departs, and honor him as a picture of calm wisdom in a child.

games.q: you're a child Guru. a proud scholar challenges you: explain the Gita, if you're really the Guru. what do you do?
o: recite it yourself to prove him wrong.
ask for a humble person from the village to explain it.

practice: Pick something ordinary: pour a glass of water, fold a shirt, wash a cup. Take three slow breaths, then do it at half speed, the way a small child does something important, feeling the weight of the cup and the sound of the water.
When it's done, sit and let that calm spread into your breathing.
